summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that the offence covers sodomy and acts involving contact between males that a reasonable person would regard as indecent. Sodomy is classified in the Criminal Code as unlawful sexual conduct, defined as anal sexual intercourse or any indecent act between consenting adults, with common-law formulations covering "unlawful and intentional sexual relations per anum between two human males" and "unnatural offences".

A 2006 revision of the Criminal Code expanded sodomy beyond sexual activity to any act involving contact between two males that a reasonable person would regard as an indecent act, and added a sexual deviancy offence covering holding hands, hugging or kissing between two people of the same sex. That amendment was one of fifteen additions made to the Code. Physical contact of that kind between two men is therefore itself chargeable, independent of any sexual act.

Gender marker change is not allowed. Section 18(2) of the Births and Deaths Registration Act permits a first-name change only on application to the Registrar General with evidence justifying the need, and the Registrar General's discretion may prevent a change based on gender identity. Activist Jordan Chanetsa is documented commenting that transgender people face difficulty accessing legal work because official documents do not reflect their gender.

Toilet access has produced a documented arrest. In 2014 activist Rikki Nathanson was arrested on a criminal nuisance charge for using a women's bathroom; the charge was thrown out, she sued for damages and won, and in 2015 she established Trans Research, Education, Advocacy & Training (TREAT). The most recent documented incident of this kind in the record is that 2014 arrest; no later instance is documented.

In July 2018 the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender and gender-nonconforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, recording that nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups, and was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff.

Health Ministry training manuals further require health professionals to support the unique healthcare needs of transgender and non-gender conforming people alongside sex workers, men who have sex with men, and people who inject and use drugs, and state that criminalisation of sex work, drug use and some sexual acts creates disproportionate harms, undermines HIV prevention for the whole nation, and impairs access to healthcare. Formal policy guarantees health-service access including transition-relevant care at public facilities, while day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under the 2018 handbook.

Same-sex marriage is banned by the Constitution, which was amended in 2013 to define marriage as between a man and a woman, and in May 2019 Cabinet approved marriage-law amendments to align the ban. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as a same-sex marriage has no route to recognition.

LGBTQ people have no general legal protections from discrimination, violence and harassment, except explicit protection based on sexual orientation regarding personal information under the Freedom of Information Act (2020) and the Cyber and Data Protection Act (2022).

Since 1995 the Government has carried out campaigns against homosexual men and women, with enforcement including infiltration of GALZ, bribery, detention, beating, killing and rape by authorities and reported use of the Central Intelligence Organisation to beat and arrest homosexuals. Section 11 of the Censorship and Entertainments Control Act, prohibiting undesirable publications defined as "indecent or obscene or is offensive or harmful to public morals or is likely to be contrary to public health", has been used to harass LGBTQ people and activists.

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990 with more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres, provides legal support explicitly covering arrests for "sodomy", counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. Legal aid and counselling remain reachable for an LGBTI traveller despite criminalisation.
tangentialFactors:
Amnesty International report of 9 January 2024, index AFR 01/7533/2024, titled "We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries", examines anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people across several African states, placing Zimbabwe's statutory regime within a wider regional pattern of legal hostility.

The most recent documented prosecution in this record is the 1998 case against former President Canaan Banana, found guilty on eleven charges of sodomy, attempted sodomy and indecent assault following a 1996 arrest, sentenced to 10 years imprisonment, defrocked, and having served 6 months in an open prison. No later prosecution is documented here.

The 2014 bathroom arrest was resolved in the complainant's favour through the courts, which shows a remedy existing alongside the criminal charge; the record does not document whether that outcome has been repeated.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the statutory penalty for sodomy or for the sexual deviancy offence, so no sentence range is given here.

No source in this inventory addresses entry and visa rules, passport gender markers, border or airport screening treatment of transgender or gender-nonconforming travellers, or document-marker flagging. Those questions are unresolved on this record.

The frequency of current enforcement is not sourced. The record documents the statutory offences, the 1995-onward campaign, the 1998 prosecution and the 2014 bathroom arrest, but supplies no prosecution counts, no period-covered figures, and no per-capita or comparative violence statistics; the absence of later incidents in this inventory is not evidence that they do not occur.

Whether the 2018 health ministry handbook remains in force, and how many practitioners have been trained under it, is not sourced. The record documents the policy and the training requirement, not coverage or compliance.

The Amnesty International report of 9 January 2024 is listed for its scope and title only; its Zimbabwe-specific findings are not reproduced in this inventory and remain unverified here.

No source addresses hate-crime provisions, custody rules, or legal recognition of gender change by court order, so those are not sourced either way.
